title: Une chanteuse pour Julien  (A Singer for Julien)

segments.t: In Gabriel's office, Gabriel excitedly tells Sofia that pop singer and client Julien Dore is arriving to discuss his musical movie. Seeking to launch Sofia's singing career, Gabriel coaches her to act like an established artist while keeping their personal life secret. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Julien Doré vient parler de son film.
Tu veux me présenter à Julien Doré?
Il cherche une chanteuse pour son film.
Charlotte Le Bon ne chante pas?
Non, elle chante très mal!
Mais toi, mon amour, tu chantes à merveille.
Il sait que je suis ta copine?
Non, tu es une cliente de l'agence.
Ne te mets pas la pression, Sofia.
Il sait que je suis réceptionniste?
Bien sûr que non, assieds-toi là.
Tu aimes vraiment Julien Doré?
Je l'adore, c'est pour ça que je panique!
Let's examine how Gabriel coaches Sofia step by step to prepare for the meeting.
Julien Doré vient parler de son film.
'Julien Dore is coming to talk about his film.' Notice there is no connector between 'comes' and 'to talk' in French—unlike 'just happened', plain 'comes to do' links straight to the next action.
Tu veux me présenter à Julien Doré?
'You want to introduce me to Julien Dore?' Watch the cognate: what looks like 'present' is the everyday French way to say 'introduce' someone, with 'me' tucked before it.
Il cherche une chanteuse pour son film.
'He is looking for a singer for his film.' One French action covers 'looks for' with no 'for' needed afterward, and the '-euse' ending marks a female singer.
Charlotte Le Bon ne chante pas?
'Charlotte Le Bon does not sing?' Keeping statement order and raising her pitch at the end lets Sofia turn a negative sentence into an incredulous question in French.
Non, elle chante très mal!
'No, she sings very badly!' Short and punchy, 'very badly' ends with a three-letter word that means 'badly' after an action or 'harm' on its own.
Mais toi, mon amour, tu chantes à merveille.
'But you, my love, you sing wonderfully.' Gabriel stresses 'you' up front before repeating casual 'you' with 'sing', and caps it with an idiom literally meaning 'to marvel'.
Il sait que je suis ta copine?
'Does he know that I am your girlfriend?' When talking about facts rather than people, French uses its fact-knowing word 'knows', while the final word can mean either 'female friend' or 'girlfriend'.
Non, tu es une cliente de l'agence.
'No, you are a client of the agency.' Adding '-e' to 'client' marks a female client—and unlike silent vowel endings, this '-e' lets you clearly hear the preceding 't' sound.
Ne te mets pas la pression, Sofia.
'Do not put pressure on yourself, Sofia.' Literally 'do not put yourself the pressure', this idiomatic coaching phrase uses 'the' before 'pressure' where English leaves it bare.
Il sait que je suis réceptionniste?
'Does he know that I am a receptionist?' Job titles after 'I am' stand without 'a' in French, so Sofia literally asks 'that I am receptionist'.
Bien sûr que non, assieds-toi là.
'Of course not, sit down there.' Literally 'well sure that no', this emphatic three-word expression is what you'd say for 'of course not!' in everyday French.
Tu aimes vraiment Julien Doré?
'Do you really like Julien Dore?' Sliding 'really' between 'like' and a person's name keeps the French action from sounding like romantic 'love'—here it means 'are you really a fan of'.
Je l'adore, c'est pour ça que je panique!

'I adore him, that is why I am panicking!' Built word-for-word as 'it is for this reason I panic', this high-energy spoken frame is how French speakers say 'that's why'. Now let's listen to the whole scene once more from start to finish.
Julien Doré vient parler de son film.
Tu veux me présenter à Julien Doré?
Il cherche une chanteuse pour son film.
Charlotte Le Bon ne chante pas?
Non, elle chante très mal!
Mais toi, mon amour, tu chantes à merveille.
Il sait que je suis ta copine?
Non, tu es une cliente de l'agence.
Ne te mets pas la pression, Sofia.
Il sait que je suis réceptionniste?
Bien sûr que non, assieds-toi là.
Tu aimes vraiment Julien Doré?
Je l'adore, c'est pour ça que je panique!

Gabriel prepares Sofia to impress Julien Dore while carefully guarding her dual identity as receptionist and girlfriend. Let's review the vocabulary and conversational expressions used in this dialogue. See you next time!
Au revoir!
